scores.rationale: The stylized fact states that energy dissipation always occurs in living systems, even anaerobically (in the absence of dioxygen). The snippets broadly affirm the general thermodynamic principle that living systems are dissipative structures that degrade free energy and increase entropy (e.g., [13], [15], [5], [7]), which is consistent with the idea that some energy always dissipates. However, none of the snippets specifically address the anaerobic/dioxygen-independent aspect of the claim, which is the distinctive content of the fact. Most snippets are general thermodynamics/origin-of-life/education abstracts that mention dissipation only at a high level, and several conflate oxidative metabolism with combustion ([9]). No snippet contradicts the fact, but support for the specific anaerobic dissipation claim is absent, leaving the evidence weak and only indirectly relevant despite the broad thermodynamic consensus.

This approach requires a particular kind of stability for these stages—dynamic kinetic stability (DKS)—which is not usually observed in regular chemistry, and which is reflected in the persistence of entities capable of self-reproduction. The necessary connection of this kinetic behaviour with far-from-equilibrium thermodynamic conditions is emphasized and this leads to an evolutionary view for the origin of life in which multiplying entities must be associated with the dissipation of free energy.

The ecodeme, or group of like individuals interacting equally within the constraints of the niche boundaries, exhibits the characteristics of a dissipative structure. The characteristics of a dissipative structure demand that it actively acquire and conserve energy, and that it exhibit organization. Organization implies the existence of order and a goal or end point; order is represented by uniformity of individuals in the ecodeme, the goal is represented by the state of least entropy production.

snippets.title: The Thermodynamic Origin of Ecosystems
snippets.label: supports
snippets.text: A general theory of the origin of ecosystems in thermodynamic terms is developed. Regular fluctuations in the availablility of energy give rise to dissipative structures in systems where the boundary constraints preclude the development of the equilibrium state. Dissipative structures are patterns in the energy flow that cease to exist when the energy flow ceases; when in the vicinity of their equilibrium position, they tend to a state of least entropy production.
